newsitem.title: USA: New data confirms U.S. economic might.
newsitem.headline: New data confirms U.S. economic might.

text.p: The nation's economy showed more signs of robust growth Thursday as a new batch of data revealed soaring homes sales, buoyant help-wanted advertising and fewer Americans entering unemployment lines.
The reports added more proof of a steadily expanding economy and fueled speculation that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates further to head off inflation.
The central bank boosted short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point on Tuesday and some economists said another rate hike could be in the offing.

"There is a logical reason for the Fed to tighten," said Tim O'Neill, chief economist for Harris Bank/Bank of Montreal. "But it doesn't have to be a major league tightening -- the Fed has to tap on the brakes but it doesn't have to jam them on."
A closely watched barometer of the job market showed there were fewer Americans lining up to collect unemployment benefits last week.

The Labor Department said first-time jobless claims fell to 310,000 in the week ended March 22, compared with a revised 314,000 the week earlier. Wall Street economists had forecast claims of 313,000.
The four-week moving average of claims, considered a more reliable gauge of trends, fell to 311,250 from a revised 312,750.
The total number of Americans continuing to claim unemployment benefits was also down, falling to 2.28 million in the week ended March 15, the latest week for which those data were available.
That was the lowest level for ongoing claims since the week ended Dec. 9, 1989, when they hit 2.27 million, the department said.
In another report, sales of previously owned homes bolted to the second highest level on record as a stable economy and relatively low interest rates helped encourage home buyers.

The National Association of Realtors said that sales of existing, or previously occupied, homes rose 9.0 percent in February to a seasonably adjusted annual rate of 4.26 million units from a revised 3.91 million in January.
The February sales rate was up 5.2 percent from sales of 4.05 million in February 1996 and reached its highest level since May 1996's record-setting 4.28 million units.
The median price of an existing home fell to $117,500 in February from $120,600 in January, but it rose from $114,000 a year ago.
The group's chief economist said he did not expect the Fed's decision this week to raise interest rates to cause a "notable decline" in home sales.
"The increase in mortgage rates won't be high enough to pull people out of the market or cause them to postpone purchasing decisions," NAR Chief Economist John Tuccillo said.
But at a news conference following the release of the report, Tuccillo said he still expected activity to level off some. "The housing market will be down over the next few months," he said.
Mortgage rates for a 30-year loan averaged 7.65 percent in February, down from 7.82 percent in January but up from 7.08 percent in February a year ago.
In other economic news, a national help-wanted advertising index rose to 90 in February from 87 in January, according to the Conference Board, a private business group.
"The job market continues to show surprising strength," Conference Board economist Ken Goldstein said.
